messages.content: Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6.

function.name: statistics_calculate_p_value
function.description: Calculate the p-value for a t-test on a single sample from a population. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

sample_mean.description: The mean of the sample data. This is a float type value.

population_mean.description: The mean of the population data. This is a float type value.

sample_std_dev.description: The standard deviation of the sample data. This is a float type value.

sample_size.description: The size of the sample data.

two_tailed.description: Whether the test is two-tailed. If not provided, default is true.

message.content:
**Standard error (standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean)**  

\[
SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{1.4}{\sqrt{40}}
    \approx \frac{1.4}{6.3249}
    \approx 0.2215
\]

So the standard deviation of the null‑hypothesis test (i.e., the standard error of the mean under the null) is **≈ 0.22**.
message.reasoning:
The user wants "the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test" given sample mean, sample std dev, sample size, population mean. They likely want the standard error of the mean under null? Standard deviation of sampling distribution of sample mean under null: sigma / sqrt(n). But we don't know population sigma; they gave sample std dev as 1.4. Usually use sample std dev as estimate of sigma. So standard error = 1.4 / sqrt(40) ≈ 1.4 / 6.3249 ≈ 0.2215. That might be answer.

But maybe they want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test statistic? For t-test, the test statistic uses sample std dev. But the standard deviation of the null distribution of t-statistic is sqrt((n-1)/(n-2))? Actually t-distribution has variance n/(n-2) if df>2. But that's not typical. They might just want the standard error.

Thus answer: about 0.2215. Provide explanation.
